title: Sex Advice for Newlyweds Take it FWIW
author: Michael Foster
summary: Foster offers Scripture-shaped counsel on marital sexuality for newly-married Christians, drawing on years of listening to couples navigate early marriage. The central framing is that a honeymoon night is training camp, not the Super Bowl—excellence in sex builds through time, attention, and patient learning of one's specific spouse. Foster addresses the psychology of desire (male desire as steady and active, female desire as more cyclical and context-dependent), practical anatomy (women's orgasm typically requires clitoral stimulation beyond intercourse), communication patterns, what kills desire (desperation, anxiety, ungratefulness), protection of the marriage bed, and seasonal rhythms of intimacy. The piece emphasizes building trust and shared history rather than performance, and frames sexual intimacy as a gift to be relished rather than rushed.
points: The honeymoon is training camp, not a performance test—excellence in sex emerges through years of patient attention to one's spouse's body, preferences, and arousal patterns, not through immediate skill.
Male and female desire express differently: men experience desire as constant and active, women as more cyclical and responsive to context—understanding these patterns prevents chronic disconnection.

A woman's availability rests on feeling safe and cared for: when a husband leads by managing household order, addressing problems, and building stability, he creates the nervous-system calm where desire can awaken.
Two things kill desire fastest—for women: desperation and anxiety; for men: ungratefulness and unresponsiveness—attending to these emotional realities matters more than any physical technique.

Protecting the marriage bed means sealing past sexual history, excluding pornography and third parties, and ensuring all activity is mutual and non-degrading—this boundary is sufficient for most couples.
quotes: Your honeymoon night is not the Sex Super Bowl. It's training camp. Day one. Two people starting to learn how to love one specific person well.

You don't know each other yet. Not really. You don't know rhythms. You don't know insecurities. You don't know what relaxes your spouse or what shuts them down. That kind of knowledge only comes with time and attention.
For most couples, the best sex of their marriage comes much later than they expect, assuming they keep working at knowing each other. Early on, people often don't even realize how unskilled they are.
Most women experience desire as more moderate, more cyclical, and often more latent. Put plainly: men are usually ready. Women often are not.

Husbands, two things shut a woman down faster than almost anything else: desperation and anxiety. Wives, two things deflate a man faster than almost anything else: ungratefulness and unresponsiveness.

Order paves the way for intimacy. Homes that are governed. Kids who are being formed. Money that's being handled. Problems that are addressed instead of avoided. When those things are neglected, anxiety fills the house. And anxiety is poison to desire.” Archived from We Made People (Foster Substack) on May 2, 2026 by Tim.
